question: What is the primary architectural difference between Git and GitHub?
options: Git is a local distributed version control software; GitHub is a cloud hosting platform for Git repositories.
Git is only for Linux; GitHub is for Windows and macOS.
Git is for writing code; GitHub is for compiling code.
There is no difference; they are different branding of the exact same program.
explanation: Git is the distributed version control tool that records file snapshots locally on your machine. GitHub is a cloud-based service that hosts Git repositories online and provides collaboration tools like Pull Requests and issue trackers.

question: What happens under the hood when you run 'git init' inside a project directory?
options: It creates a git.exe binary in the current folder.
It creates a hidden '.git' directory containing repository metadata, object database, and config.
It deletes all untracked files in the folder.
It automatically uploads your code to GitHub.
explanation: 'git init' creates a hidden '.git' folder in your directory. This folder stores all commit history, Git configuration, hooks, and object databases.

question: What are the three core areas or trees of a local Git project?
options: Local Drive, USB Drive, and Cloud Backup
Master, Main, and Origin
Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), and Repository (HEAD commit history)
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
explanation: Git manages files across three areas: the Working Directory (untracked/modified files on disk), the Staging Area / Index (prepared snapshot), and the Repository (.git history storing permanent commits).

question: You modified README.md and ran 'git commit -m "Fix docs"', but Git said 'no changes added to commit'. Why?
options: Git requires you to push before you can commit.
The commit message must be at least 50 characters.
You cannot commit files with a .md extension.
The modified file was not staged with 'git add README.md' before committing.
explanation: Git requires changes to be explicitly moved from the working directory into the staging area using 'git add' before 'git commit' can record them in a new snapshot.

question: Which command displays the current branch name, uncommitted changes, staged files, and untracked files?
options: git status
git branch --check
git log
git show
explanation: 'git status' gives a comprehensive status report of your active branch, staged files (green), unstaged modifications (red), and untracked files.

question: What is a Git branch conceptually?
options: A completely duplicated folder copy of your entire hard drive.
A lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit snapshot.
A remote cloud server hosted by Microsoft.
A zip file generated at every commit.
explanation: In Git, a branch is simply a lightweight movable pointer (a 41-byte text file containing a 40-character commit SHA-1 hash) pointing to the latest commit of that line of development.

question: What is the recommended modern Git command to create a branch named 'feature-auth' and switch to it in one step?
options: git goto feature-auth
git merge -c feature-auth
git switch -c feature-auth
git branch -make feature-auth
explanation: 'git switch -c <branch-name>' was introduced in Git 2.23 to cleanly separate branch switching from file restoration. (The older equivalent is 'git checkout -b <branch-name>').

question: Why should developers create feature branches instead of committing directly to 'main'?
options: Because GitHub charges money for commits made directly on main.
Branches make your computer run faster.
Because Git will crash if you make more than 5 commits on main.
To isolate unfinished work so the production 'main' branch remains stable and deployable.
explanation: Branching isolates experimental or in-progress features. If something breaks on a feature branch, 'main' remains healthy, tested, and releasable.

question: What is a 'Fast-Forward' merge in Git?
options: A merge where main simply moves its pointer forward because no divergent commits were made on main.
A merge performed over 5G internet.
A merge that automatically resolves all merge conflicts without human input.
A merge that skips code reviews and unit tests.
explanation: A fast-forward merge occurs when there is a linear path from the target branch to the feature branch. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward without needing a merge commit.

question: What happens when you run 'git merge feature' while checked out on 'main', and divergent commits exist on both branches?
options: Git deletes all commits made on main.
Git performs a 3-way merge and creates a new 'Merge commit' uniting the two histories.
Git automatically deletes the feature branch without warning.
Git converts the repository into a Subversion repository.
explanation: When histories diverge, Git uses the common ancestor and the two branch tips to perform a 3-way merge, creating a new merge commit with two parent commits.

question: What primarily causes a merge conflict in Git?
options: When two teammates have the same first name.
When the repository exceeds 100 megabytes.
When two branches modify the exact same lines of a file differently, and Git cannot automatically decide which version to keep.
When you commit without internet access.
explanation: A merge conflict occurs when opposing changes are made to the same lines of a file, or one branch deletes a file that another branch modified. Git halts and asks a human to resolve the ambiguity.

question: In a conflicted file, what does the marker '<<<<<<< HEAD' indicate?
options: Code written by a GitHub administrator.
The end of the conflict section.
A syntax error in your programming language compiler.
The start of the changes from the branch you are currently checked out on.
explanation: '<<<<<<< HEAD' marks the beginning of the version on your currently checked-out branch. The '=======' separates your version from the incoming branch's version ('>>>>>>> branch-name').

question: After manually editing a conflicted file to keep the desired code and removing conflict markers, what must you run to finalize the merge?
options: git add <file> followed by git commit
git cancel-conflict
git checkout --force
git clean -fdx
explanation: Once conflict markers are resolved, you stage the resolved file with 'git add <file>' and run 'git commit' (or 'git merge --continue') to record the completed merge commit.

question: What is a Pull Request (PR) on GitHub or GitLab?
options: A command that downloads all files as a ZIP archive.
A formal proposal to review, discuss, and merge code changes from a branch into a target branch.
A notification sent to delete a repository.
A request to download git.exe onto your laptop.
explanation: A Pull Request (or Merge Request) is a collaborative review workflow where team members view diffs, leave inline comments, run automated CI checks, and approve changes before merging.

question: What is the difference between 'git clone' and 'Forking' on GitHub?
options: Cloning is for open-source; Forking is only for private code.
Cloning deletes the original repository; Forking duplicates it.
Cloning copies a repo to your local computer; Forking creates an independent server-side copy under your GitHub account.
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same operation.
explanation: Forking creates an online copy of someone else's repository under your GitHub account so you can propose PRs without write access. Cloning downloads a repository from the web onto your local machine.

question: What does the '-u' (or '--set-upstream') flag do in 'git push -u origin feature'?
options: It forces the push even if it causes data loss.
It creates an urgent high-priority commit.
It unzips files on GitHub.
It links your local 'feature' branch to 'origin/feature' so future 'git push' and 'git pull' know where to sync.
explanation: The '-u' flag configures upstream tracking. Once configured, Git knows which remote branch corresponds to your local branch, allowing you to just type 'git push' or 'git pull'.

question: What is the key difference between 'git fetch' and 'git pull'?
options: 'git fetch' downloads new remote commits without merging them into your branch; 'git pull' runs fetch AND merges them immediately.
'git fetch' only works for README files; 'git pull' works for code.
'git fetch' deletes local branches that don't match GitHub.
'git fetch' is for uploading; 'git pull' is for downloading.
explanation: 'git fetch' safely downloads remote commits, updating remote tracking branches (like origin/main) without touching your working files. 'git pull' performs 'git fetch' + 'git merge' in one go.

question: You try to run 'git push' and receive '[rejected - non-fast-forward]'. What is the most common reason?
options: The file names contain spaces.
The remote branch has newer commits made by teammates that you have not pulled yet.
Your laptop battery is below 20%.
Git does not allow commits with emojis.
explanation: A non-fast-forward rejection happens when GitHub has commits that do not exist in your local branch. To fix it, run 'git pull' to integrate remote changes first, then push.

question: You made unintended changes in 'app.js' that you have NOT staged yet. How do you discard them and restore the last committed version?
options: git remove app.js
git uncommit app.js
git restore app.js
git delete app.js
explanation: In modern Git, 'git restore <file>' discards uncommitted changes in the working tree, reverting the file back to the last committed state.

question: You ran 'git add secret.env' by mistake. Which command un-stages it without deleting your local changes?
options: git branch -d secret.env
git erase secret.env
git rm secret.env
git restore --staged secret.env
explanation: 'git restore --staged <file>' (or older 'git reset HEAD <file>') removes the file from the staging area while leaving your file contents untouched in your working directory.

question: You are halfway through a feature, but your team needs an urgent hotfix on 'main'. How do you temporarily shelve your uncommitted work without committing junk?
options: git stash
git pause
git hide
git sleep
explanation: 'git stash' takes your dirty working tree and staged changes and saves them onto a temporary stack, giving you a clean working directory. Later, run 'git stash pop' to restore your work.

question: Which command retrieves and reapplies your most recently stashed changes onto your current branch?
options: git stash paste
git stash pop
git unstash
git stash restore-all
explanation: 'git stash pop' applies the top stash to your working directory and removes it from your stash stack list.

question: Which command displays a compact, single-line-per-commit visual ASCII graph of project branch history?
options: git branch --ascii
git tree --view
git log --oneline --graph --all
git diagram
explanation: 'git log --oneline --graph --all' renders a clean text-based graph showing branch divergence, commits, and merge points across the entire repository.

question: What does 'git diff' (without any flags) show you?
options: The differences between two different users.
The differences between GitHub and your local drive.
The files deleted in the last 10 days.
The exact line-by-line differences between your working directory and the staging area.
explanation: 'git diff' inspects unstaged modifications—showing what you have changed in your files but not yet staged with 'git add'.

question: What is the purpose of a '.gitignore' file?
options: To tell Git which files, folders, build artifacts, or secret keys to deliberately exclude from tracking.
To ignore compiler warnings in your code.
To ignore pull requests from specific users.
To block unauthorized internet access to your machine.
explanation: A '.gitignore' text file patterns files and directories (like node_modules, .env, *.log, build/) that Git should never track or prompt you to commit.

question: What is the purpose of setting 'git config --global user.name' and 'user.email'?
options: To create your GitHub password.
To attribute authorship and identity to every commit you make in Git.
To register your laptop with the Linux foundation.
To license your open-source software under MIT.
explanation: Every commit in Git permanently stores the author's name and email address. Configuring these ensures your commits are properly attributed to you on GitHub.

question: What is HEAD in Git?
options: The GitHub server's CPU processor.
The very first commit ever made in the project.
A special symbolic reference pointing to the currently checked-out commit or branch tip.
The top line of a README.md file.
explanation: HEAD is a pointer that determines what commit or branch is currently active in your working directory. Normally HEAD points to a branch name, which in turn points to a commit.

question: What does it mean when Git displays the message 'You are in 'detached HEAD' state'?
options: The remote repository on GitHub has been deleted.
Your Git installation is corrupted and must be reinstalled.
Git has stopped tracking files on your laptop.
HEAD is pointing directly to a specific commit hash rather than a named branch.
explanation: Detached HEAD occurs when you checkout a specific commit hash or tag instead of a branch. If you make new commits in this state, they won't belong to any branch unless you create one (e.g., 'git switch -c new-branch').

question: In Git remote commands, what does the word 'origin' represent by convention?
options: The default nickname/alias for the remote repository URL that was cloned or linked.
The root directory of your hard drive (/ or C:\).
The main software license file.
The computer manufacturer where the code originated.
explanation: 'origin' is simply the standard default alias given to the remote repository URL when you clone a repository or link one with 'git remote add origin <url>'.

question: Which of the following is considered a best practice for Git commit messages?
options: Copy and paste the entire source file contents into the message.
Write a concise, imperative summary (e.g. 'Add search filter to products API') explaining what the commit does.
Commit 2,000 files at once with message 'stuff' or 'fixes'.
Always leave the commit message blank so coworkers can inspect the diff.
explanation: Good commit messages explain why a change was made in a clear, imperative tone (e.g., 'Fix memory leak in image loader'). This helps team members and future contributors understand project history.

question: What is the primary difference between 'git reset --hard' and 'git revert'?
options: 'git revert' deletes the entire repository.
They are identical commands with different spelling.
'git reset --hard' rewrites history by moving the branch pointer back and deleting changes; 'git revert' creates a new commit that safely inverts the changes.
'git reset' is only for text files; 'git revert' is only for images.
explanation: 'git reset --hard' rewrites commit history (dangerous for shared public branches). 'git revert' safely undoes changes by appending a brand new commit that cancels out the previous commit's diff.

question: After your feature branch has been reviewed and merged into main, how do you safely delete the local branch?
options: git delete branch feature-branch
git erase -b feature-branch
git rm feature-branch
git branch -d feature-branch
explanation: 'git branch -d <branch>' safely deletes a local branch. If the branch contains unmerged changes, Git will protect you by requiring an uppercase '-D' to force deletion.

question: Which command removes a remote tracking reference locally if a branch was deleted on GitHub?
options: git fetch --prune
git clean -fd
git remote --scrub
git delete-orphans
explanation: 'git fetch --prune' (or 'git fetch -p') contacts the remote and cleans up stale local tracking references for branches that no longer exist on GitHub.

question: What does 'Squash and Merge' do when accepting a Pull Request on GitHub?
options: Compresses the files into a .tar.gz archive.
Combines all commits from the feature branch into a single clean commit on the target branch.
Merges code while skipping CI tests.
Deletes all images in the pull request to save bandwidth.
explanation: Squash merging condenses all the minor 'work in progress' commits from a feature branch into one clean, unified commit before adding it to main, keeping the main log tidy.

question: What algorithm does Git use to generate its 40-character commit hashes?
options: RSA
MD5
SHA-1 (with newer versions supporting SHA-256)
AES-256
explanation: Git uses cryptographic hashing (historically SHA-1, with modern transition to SHA-256) to produce unique 40-character checksums that represent commits, trees, and blobs based on their exact contents.
